topic.title: Learning-Augmented Online Algorithms and Scheduling
topic.overview: Online systems must make decisions before future requests, job lengths, or resource demands are known. Learning-augmented algorithms use predictions to improve these choices while studying what happens when the predictions fail. The central concepts are consistency with accurate advice, robustness to inaccurate advice, and the cost of acquiring or combining predictions.
topic.whyItMatters: This framework makes prediction errors part of algorithm design rather than an afterthought. It is especially useful for scheduling and caching, where an attractive average forecast can otherwise produce poor worst-case behavior. Performance claims depend on the problem model and the available feedback.
topic.evolution: Early representative titles concern queue-delay prediction and job scheduling in the 1990s. A 2020 analysis establishes tight robustness-consistency trade-offs for ski rental and scheduling. Subsequent work considers explicit predictors, mixed advice, and query budgets; 2026 representatives extend the practical setting to language-model inference scheduling and resource-aware training-loss prediction.
openQuestions: Which prediction errors matter most for each scheduling objective?
How should a system allocate a limited budget for querying or updating advice?
